segments.caption: We turned Bangalore localities into numbers. Whitefield 1, up to Koramangala 5.
And our model decided Koramangala is 5 times Whitefield.
Those numbers were just name tags, but the model did maths on them. To it, Whitefield plus Whitefield equals Hebbal.
Day 8 of 100 Days of Machine Learning: encoding categories. 2 kinds of categories, 6 methods, and the trap that leaks your answers.
Models only understand numbers, so every text column needs encoding. First, know which kind you have.
Nominal: no order, like locality or facing direction. Ordinal: a real order, like unfurnished, semi furnished, fully furnished.
The beginner move is label encoding: give each category a number.
On localities, that invents a fake order. Linear models and KNN treat the gaps as real distances. Tree models cope better, but don't count on it.
Method 1: ordinal encoding.
For ordered categories, set the order yourself. Unfurnished 0, semi 1, fully 2. Never let the computer sort them alphabetically.
Method 2: one-hot encoding.
For localities, make one column per locality. A 1 where it matches, 0s everywhere else. No fake order, no fake distances.
Method 3: drop one column.
If every other column is 0, you already know it's the last one. So for linear regression, keep k minus 1 columns. Skip this, and you fall into the dummy variable trap.
Method 4: group the rare ones.
Bangalore has over 200 localities. One-hot gives you 200 mostly empty columns. Keep the common ones, and group localities with only a few listings into OTHER.
Method 5: target encoding.
Replace each locality with its average price per sq ft. One powerful column instead of 200. Smooth it, so a locality with 2 listings doesn't get an extreme value.
Method 6: plan for unseen categories.
Next month, a listing arrives from a brand new locality your model has never seen. Map unknowns to OTHER, or your code crashes in production.
Now the trap that leaks your answers.
Target encoding uses the price, the very thing you predict. Calculate the averages on training data only, ideally out of fold. Use the whole dataset, and the model peeks at the test answers.
So here's the decision guide.
Ordered? Ordinal encoding. Few categories? One-hot, and drop one for linear models. Too many? Group the rare ones, or target encode. Always handle unseen categories. And fit on training data only.
Save this. You'll need it in every project.
